20001-the-english-spy:
The English Spy was a Regency satire drawn by Robert Cruikshank, published in 1825 and 1826. Its motto promises frolic, mirth, and fancy, with Old Father Time borne away. The writer threatens to dish up a meal of London low life. He craves abuse enough from offended readers, he jokes. Bernard Blackmantle, the spy's persona, prowled clubs, prisons, and gaming rooms. Charles Molloy Westmacott wrote the sketches behind that mask.

The English Spy copied Pierce Egan's Life in London formula. Cruikshank's plates of rakes and rogues made it famous. Its London is drunk, indebted, and theatrical at all hours. Regency satire this broad needs its pictures close by. The book remains a key source for Georgian nightlife. Few satires smell so strongly of their streets.
22775-psychotherapy:
Hugo Münsterberg wrote Psychotherapy, a 1909 book arguing that mental healing belongs to psychology and must rest on a science of the mind. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Münsterberg, Harvard's famous psychologist, wrote as suggestion cures, faith healing, and Freud's new talk of the unconscious competed for the public.

Psychotherapy's only safe basis, he begins, is a thorough knowledge of human personality, gained through psychology. Yet the claim means nothing until we are clear what psychological knowledge is. We can know man in many ways. The book works out his answer: the mind as a causal system, treated by a trained psychologist, not by mystics. It is a founding text of clinical psychology's claim to its own territory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-canopy:
The altar canopy, or baldachinum, hangs over the altar, square in form and large enough to cover altar and predella. Its silk, velvet, or other cloth should match the altar ornaments in colour when easily done. It hangs by a movable chain from the ceiling, or attaches to wall or reredos. It may stand as a marble, stone, metal, or wood cupola on four pillars, called in liturgy the ciborium.

Rulings require it over the Blessed Sacrament altar and other altars, yet custom, even in Rome, limits it mostly to the high altar and the Blessed Sacrament altar. Its purpose is to shield the altar from dust falling from high ceilings that cannot be cleaned conveniently. On solemn festivals a temporary canopy sometimes rises over an altar indoors or outside, its frame called the altar-herse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canopy: A 1913 entry on the canopy — the baldachin of honor. Patrick Morrisroe explains its solemn use. The silk shelters the Blessed Sacrament. The procession bears its fourfold poles. The honor of the carried Host. Its poles are borne by the deacons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psychotherapy: Psychotherapy is the healing of the mind by the mind's own powers. This entry examines its methods and the Catholic judgment. The cure of souls by speech: its quiet couch hears the troubled confession of suffering souls in pain and doubt.

my-adventures-as-a-spy:
Lieut.-Gen. Sir Robert Baden-Powell tells true tales of his own spying here. Pearson issued the book in London in 1915. Baden-Powell drew the pictures himself. He was famed as founder of the Boy Scouts and author of Scouting for Boys.

The tales draw on his years as a soldier and scout. Disguise, codes, and close watching fill the pages. He writes for boys who love detective tales and woodcraft. Press quotes praise the book as a fine gift for schoolboys. It shows how a scout's skills, tracking, sketching, and calm nerve, served a spy in the field before the Great War.
the-spy:
Richard Harding Davis tells this tale through a narrator, Mr. Crosby, who insists that his going to Valencia was entirely an accident. Nobody at the capital believes him. The American minister presses him after dinner for the secret game. The minister's wife scolds him for not trusting her husband. She then spreads word that he works for the Walker-Keefe crowd.

Crosby explains that the State Department sent him to Panama to straighten out a conflict in the canal zone, where yellow fever brought quarantines that closed every useful port. Valencia alone had a direct line to New York. Yet a man named Schnitzel disbelieved the accident, followed him home, and through that pursuit the spy's own story comes to be told.
